uncited: - **Input:** The view direction vector $\mathbf{v}$ (from camera to sample point), the surface normal $\mathbf{n}$ at the sample point (or the ray direction relative to the volume orientation if normals are not explicitly stored), and the base opacity $\alpha_{base}$ derived from the transfer function.
No additional complex data structures are required beyond those in standard DVR.
The method relies on the geometric relationship between the viewing ray and the local geometry.
**Compute Incidence Angle:** Determine the angle $\theta$ between the view direction $\mathbf{v}$ and the normal $\mathbf{n}$ at the current sample point.
where $\mathbf{v}$ is the vector from the camera to the sample point, and $\mathbf{n}$ is the normal at that point.
**Calculate Transparency Factor:** Compute a transparency factor $T(\theta)$ that decreases as the angle becomes more grazing (i.e., as $\theta$ approaches 90 degrees or $\pi/2$ radians).
If $|\cos \theta|$ is small (grazing angle), $T(\theta)$ is small, making the sample more transparent.
If $|\cos \theta|$ is large (head-on), $T(\theta)$ is large, preserving opacity.
Alternatively, some implementations use the factor to modulate the transmittance directly.
- **Threshold:** A minimum opacity value may be enforced to prevent complete transparency in very grazing angles, avoiding noise amplification.
- **Time Complexity:** Adds a constant-time geometric calculation (dot product and power function) per sample.
Negligible overhead compared to sampling and compositing.
- **Memory Complexity:** No additional memory required if normals are computed on the fly from gradients.
If normals are precomputed, additional memory for normal vectors is needed.
The concept of view-dependent transparency was introduced to enhance the visual quality of volumetric data, particularly in medical visualization and real-time rendering of complex scenes.
